en: The Benevolent Kings’ Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra for Protecting the State,
Volume One. By Kai-fu Yi-tong San-si, Te-jin, Shi Hong-lu Qing, Duke of Su with a fief of three thousand households,
recipient of purple robes, posthumously titled Minister of Works, and canonically named Dajian (Great Mirror).
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Amoghavajra, Dharma Master of Great Wisdom at Daxingshan Monastery, by Imperial Decree. Chapter One: The Introduction Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of one thousand eight hundred bhikṣus. All were arhats whose outflows were exhausted and who were free from further afflictions; their minds were well-liberated and their wisdom was well-liberated. They had accomplished what was to be done through the nine knowledges and ten knowledges, and had mastered the contemplations of the three provisional and real [teachings] and the three gates of emptiness.
They had fully perfected both conditioned merits and unconditioned merits. Furthermore, there was an assembly of eight hundred bhikṣuṇīs, all of whom were arhats.

Furthermore, there were immeasurable and innumerable bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who had eternally severed the hindrances of delusion through the equality of true wisdom; who, through skillful means, gave rise to great practices and vows, benefiting sentient beings with the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) and universally covering all with the four immeasurable minds (*apramāṇa*); who had attained mastery through the three insights (*trividyā*) and acquired the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*); who cultivated boundless factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*) and whose craftsmanship and arts surpassed those of the world; who had deeply entered into dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*); who entered and emerged from the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) while manifesting immeasurable displays; who subdued the enmity of Māra and simultaneously illuminated the two truths (*satyadvaya*); who possessed the Dharma-eye that universally perceives and knows the faculties of sentient beings; who fearlessly expounded the Dharma through the four kinds of unimpeded understanding (*pratisaṃvid*); who possessed the thunderous sound of the Dharma through the sublime wisdom of the ten powers (*daśabala*); and who drew near to the peerless Vajra-samādhi—all such merits as these they fully possessed.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable assemblies of upāsakas and upāsikās, all of whom had seen the Noble Truths;

there were also immeasurable numbers practicing the seven limbs of the path of the virtuous, the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, and the powers, as well as the eight stages of mastery, the ten universal bases, and the sixteen mental applications leading to the realization of the truths.
There were also sixteen great kings—such as King Prasenajit—each accompanied by several tens of millions of followers.
Furthermore, there were the six kings of the desire realm—Śakra Devānām Indra and the others—accompanied by their retinues of immeasurable devaputras;
the great Brahmā kings of the four dhyānas of the form realm, also accompanied by their retinues of immeasurable devaputras;
and the immeasurable sentient beings of the various destinies who undergo transformation, such as the asuras and others, together with their diverse retinues.
Furthermore, he manifested the pure lands of the ten directions and produced ten billion lion thrones, upon which the Buddha sat and extensively proclaimed the essentials of the Dharma.
Before each throne, a single flower appeared; these ten billion flowers were adorned with a multitude of precious jewels.
Upon each of the flowers, there were again immeasurable transformation Buddhas and immeasurable Bodhisattvas, with the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings all being immeasurable.
Among them, each Buddha proclaimed the Prajñāpāramitā, which circulated and pervaded the Buddha-lands of the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
There were such great assemblies of those who had come, each of whom prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.

At that time, on the eighth day of the first month, the World-Honored One entered the Great Quiescent and Sublime Samādhi; from all the pores of his body, he emitted a great radiance that universally illuminated Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions.

At that time, immeasurable devas of the desire realm rained down various exquisite flowers, and the devas of the form realm also rained down celestial blossoms; their myriad colors intermingled, creating a scene most delightful to behold.

At that time, various fragrant flowers rained down from the formless realm; the fragrance was like Mount Sumeru and the flowers were like chariot wheels. They descended like clouds, completely covering the great assembly, while the entire Buddha-world shook in six ways.
At that time, the great assembly said to one another:

"The Greatly Awakened World-Honored One has previously taught us the Mahāprajñāpāramitā, the Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā, the Devaparipṛcchā-prajñāpāramitā, the Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā, and countless, innumerable other Prajñāpāramitās."
"Today the Tathāgata has emitted a great radiance; what deed does he intend to perform?
At that time, King Prasenajit of Śrāvastī thought to himself:
"Now the Buddha manifests this rare sign; he will surely rain down the Dharma-rain for the universal benefit and happiness of all."
He then asked the lay practitioners such as Ratnacchattra and Vimalakīrti, the great śrāvakas such as Śāriputra and Subhūti, and the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas such as Maitreya and Siṃhanāda, saying:
"What is the significance of this auspicious sign manifested by the Tathāgata?"
At that time, none among the great assembly were able to answer.

King Prasenajit and others, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, performed extensive musical performances; the various devas of the desire and form realms each played immeasurable celestial music, the sound of which pervaded the trichiliocosm.

At that time, the World-Honored One again emitted immeasurable, incalculable rays of light, their brilliance a mixture of various colors. Within each ray appeared precious lotus flowers; each flower had a thousand petals, all of golden hue, upon which transformation Buddhas sat, proclaiming the essentials of the Dharma.
This radiance of the Buddha pervades the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, appearing wherever there are those with whom he has a karmic connection.
Within those Buddha-lands of other directions—specifically, in the east, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantaprabha;
in the southeast, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Padmahasta; in the south, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vigatāśoka; and in the west...
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Light of the South, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Practice of Wisdom of the West,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Jewel Victorious of the Northwest, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Supreme Reception of the North,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Free from Dust of the Northeast, and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Joyful Reception of the Above.
Then, from the region below, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Padmavijaya and others, each accompanied by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas,
all came to this place. Carrying various kinds of incense and scattering various kinds of flowers,
they performed immeasurable musical offerings to the Tathāgata, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit silently.
With palms joined in reverence, they single-mindedly contemplate the Buddha.

**Chapter Two: Contemplating the Tathāgata** *The Benevolent Kings’ Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra for the Protection of the State* At that time, the World-Honored One arose from samādhi, sat upon the lion throne, and addressed the great assembly, saying:
"I know that the sixteen kings and their retinues have all formed this thought:"
“The World-Honored One is greatly compassionate, universally bringing benefit and joy to all.
How, O sons of good family, should we, the various kings, protect our kingdoms?
“Sons of good family! [The Buddha replied:]”
I shall now first, for the sake of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, explain the protection of the fruit of Buddhahood and the protection of the practices of the ten stages.
You all should listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well.
At that time, the great assembly—including King Prasenajit and others—having heard the Buddha’s words, all praised him together, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!”
He immediately scattered immeasurable, exquisite jewel-flowers, which transformed in mid-air into a jeweled canopy that covered the entire assembly without exception.
At that time, King Prasenajit rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, joined his palms, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva protect the fruit of buddhahood?
How does he protect the practices of the ten stages?
The Buddha addressed King Prasenajit, saying:

“Those who protect the fruit of Buddhahood—namely, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas—should abide in this manner to teach and transform all beings born from eggs, from wombs, from moisture, and by transformation. They do not contemplate the characteristics of form, nor do they contemplate the suchness of form; and it is likewise for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; for the notions of self, person, knower, and viewer; for the inversions of permanence, pleasure, purity, and self; for the four means of attraction, the six perfections, the two truths and four truths, the powers, the fearlessnesses, and all other practices, even up to the bodhisattvas and Tathāgatas themselves—they do not contemplate their characteristics, nor do they contemplate their suchness.”
Why is this? Because the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) is itself reality;

they neither come nor go, neither arise nor cease. They are identical to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), equal to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), non-dual and undifferentiated like space. Within the characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), there is no self (*ātman*) and nothing belonging to a self (*ātmīya*).
"This is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
King Prasenajit addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“If the nature of bodhisattvas and sentient beings is non-dual, by what characteristics does a bodhisattva transform sentient beings?
The Buddha said,
“Great King!”
Form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are permanent, blissful, self, and pure; the dharma-nature does not abide in form, nor does it abide in non-form.
Sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are permanent, blissful, self, and pure; likewise, they do not abide in purity, nor do they abide in non-purity.

Why is this? Because the nature of all phenomena is entirely empty; yet, by virtue of conventional truth and the three types of designation, all sentient beings possess the factors of the aggregates, bases, and elements, as well as the causes and effects of meritorious, non-meritorious, and immovable formations.
"Great King! All practices cultivated by the noble ones of the Three Vehicles, up to and including the fruit of Buddhahood, are called 'existence.
Even the sixty-two views are called 'existence.'"

"If one becomes attached to names and characteristics and discriminates among all phenomena—the six destinies, the four modes of birth, and the practices and fruits of the three vehicles—this is precisely not seeing the true nature of all phenomena.
King Prasenajit addressed the Buddha, saying, "The true nature of all phenomena is pure and equal; it is neither existent nor non-existent. How does wisdom illuminate it?"
The Buddha said,
“Great King!
Wisdom illuminates the true nature, which is neither existent nor non-existent.”
Why is this? Because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is empty.
This refers to form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; the twelve bases (āyatana); and the eighteen elements (dhātu).
The six elements of a person, the twelve links of dependent origination, the two truths, the four truths—all are empty.
These dharmas are equal in that they arise and perish simultaneously, and exist and are empty simultaneously; moment by moment, it is likewise so.
Why is this? Because within a single thought-moment there are ninety kṣaṇas, and each kṣaṇa undergoes nine hundred arisings and ceasings; thus, all conditioned phenomena are entirely empty.
By means of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one perceives that all phenomena are entirely empty:

internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, beginningless emptiness, absolute emptiness, dispersed emptiness, essential emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of *prajñāpāramitā* itself, causal emptiness, and the emptiness of the fruit of Buddhahood.
It is empty because of emptiness.

All conditioned phenomena exist through the accumulation of dharmas, exist through the accumulation of sensation, exist through the accumulation of names, exist through the accumulation of causes, exist through the accumulation of effects, exist by virtue of the six destinies, exist by virtue of the ten stages, and exist by virtue of the fruit of Buddhahood; thus, all things exist.

“Good son! If a bodhisattva dwells in the marks of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa), harboring the mark of a self (ātman), the mark of a person (pudgala), or the cognition and vision of a sentient being (sattva), they dwell in the world and are therefore not a bodhisattva.”
Why is this? Because all dharmas are entirely empty.
If one attains immovability regarding all dharmas—neither arising nor ceasing, neither possessing marks nor being markless—one should not give rise to views.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are suchness;
the Buddhas, the Dharma, and the Sangha are also suchness.
The first moment when noble wisdom manifests is endowed with eighty-four thousand pāramitās; it is called the Stage of Joy (pramuditā-bhūmi).
When obstructions are exhausted and liberation attained, that which carries one across is called a vehicle (yāna).
When the signs of movement cease, it is called the Vajra Samādhi.
The equality of essence and characteristics is called the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
"Great King!
These words and phrases of the Prajñāpāramitā have been spoken in common by hundreds of Buddhas, thousands of Buddhas, and hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of all Buddhas."

If someone were to fill as many trichiliocosm world-systems as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River with the seven treasures and offer them in alms, such that every sentient being within those great trichiliocosms attained the fruit of arhatship;

this would not equal the merit of someone who, regarding this sutra, gives rise to even a single thought of pure faith—how much more so for one who is able to receive, uphold, read, recite, or understand even a single phrase!
Why is this? Because the nature of syllables is detached;
they possess no characteristics of syllables, being neither dharmas nor non-dharmas.
Since prajñā is empty, the bodhisattva is also empty.
Why is this? Within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), each stage possesses an initial birth, a dwelling birth, and a final birth;
these thirty births are all empty, and the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*) is likewise entirely empty.
“Great King!
If a bodhisattva perceives objects, perceives wisdom, perceives speech, or perceives reception, this is not the noble vision; it is the vision of a fool.

The retributive fruits of sentient beings within the three realms are illusory—the various karmas produced by conceptualization in the desire realm, the karma produced by the four dhyānas of the form realm, and the karma produced by the four emptiness-concentrations of the formless realm. The karmic fruits of the three modes of existence are entirely empty, and the fundamental ignorance of the three realms is likewise empty.”

The outflow-free arising and ceasing of the various stages of the noble positions, as well as the remaining habitual tendencies of ignorance within the three realms and the retributive fruits of transformation, are likewise all empty.
When a Bodhisattva at the stage of Equal Enlightenment attains the Vajra-like Samādhi, the causes and effects of the two types of death are empty, and even omniscience itself is empty.

The Buddha’s unsurpassed awakening and the perfection of the knowledge of all modes are the true and pure dharma-realm of both analytical and non-analytical cessation; their nature and characteristics are equal, and even their functional application is empty. "Good son!
If there are those who practice the perfection of wisdom, whether as speakers or listeners, they are like illusory beings—there is neither speaking nor listening.
All phenomena are identical to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), just like space; all dharmas are suchness (tathatā).
"Great King!
Such is the manner in which a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva protects the fruit of Buddhahood.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed King Prasenajit, saying:
“By what marks do you perceive the Tathāgata?
King Prasenajit replied, “I perceive the true mark of the body;
my perception of the Buddha is likewise: there is no prior limit, no posterior limit, and no middle limit; it does not abide within the three limits, yet it is not separate from the three limits.”
Not abiding in the five aggregates, yet not departing from the five aggregates;
not abiding in the four great elements, yet not departing from the four great elements;
not abiding in the six sense bases, yet not departing from the six sense bases.
Not abiding in the three realms yet not departing from the three realms;
not abiding in the directions yet not departing from the directions;
clarity and ignorance are neither identical nor different.
Neither this nor that;
neither pure nor defiled;
neither conditioned nor unconditioned.
It has no self-characteristic and no other-characteristic;
it is without name and without mark;
it is without strength and without weakness.
Without demonstration and without exposition;
neither giving nor stinginess;
neither precept-keeping nor transgression.
Neither patience nor anger;
neither diligence nor indolence;
neither concentration nor distraction.
Neither wise nor foolish;
neither coming nor going;
neither entering nor exiting.
Neither a field of merit nor not a field of merit;
neither with marks nor without marks;
neither grasping nor abandoning.
Neither great nor small;
neither seen, nor heard, nor sensed, nor known;
where the movements of the mind cease and the path of language is cut off.
"Identical with the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) and equal to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā)— it is by these characteristics that I contemplate the Tathāgata.
The Buddha said, "Good son!"
It is as you have said.

The powers, fearlessnesses, and other meritorious qualities of the Buddhas, Tathāgatas—as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, as well as all their unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma)—are all likewise so.
One who cultivates the Prajñāpāramitā should contemplate them in this way; if one contemplates them otherwise, it is called a false contemplation.
When this Dharma was being taught, an immeasurable multitude attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
At that time, King Prasenajit addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva who protects the practices of the ten stages cultivate their practice?
How should they transform sentient beings?
Furthermore, by what characteristics should they abide and observe?
The Buddha told the Great King:
"All Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas rely upon the Dharma of the Five Patiences as their practice. These are:

the Patience of Subjugation, the Patience of Faith, the Patience of Accordance, and the Patience of Non-arising—each having superior, middling, and inferior grades—and within the Patience of Quiescence there are likewise superior and inferior grades; this is called the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of the Prajñāpāramitā."

Good son! At the stage of the initial subduing patience (*kṣānti*), one gives rise to the nature of the seeds of cultivation (*śikṣā-bīja-gotra*) and practices the ten stages of conduct (*daśa-caryā*).

Regarding the characteristics of the first arousal of the mind (*prathama-cittotpāda*): there are sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges who, upon seeing the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, give rise to the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), namely:

The mind of faith, the mind of mindfulness, the mind of diligence, the mind of wisdom, the mind of concentration, the mind of non-retrogression, the mind of precepts, the mind of vows, the mind of protecting the Dharma, and the mind of dedication.

Possessing these ten minds and being able to transform sentient beings even slightly, one surpasses all the wholesome stages of the two vehicles; this constitutes the Bodhisattva’s first stage of nurturing the mind, for it serves as the embryo of the noble ones.
"Furthermore, a bodhisattva of the nature-lineage (gotra) practices the ten perfections (pāramitā) and gives rise to ten remedies, namely:
observing the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena as impure, suffering, impermanent, and non-self;
counteracting the three unwholesome roots of greed, hatred, and delusion by giving rise to the three wholesome roots of generosity, loving-kindness, and wisdom."
He contemplates the patience regarding past causes across the three periods of time, the patience regarding present causes and effects, and the patience regarding future effects.

At this stage, the Bodhisattva extensively benefits sentient beings, transcending the notions of a self, a person, and a sentient being, such that he cannot be undermined by the inverted views of non-Buddhists.

"Furthermore, the Bodhisattva of the lineage of the path-practices cultivates the ten dedications and gives rise to the ten types of patient acceptance (*kṣānti*). That is to say, by contemplating the five aggregates—form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—he attains the patience of morality, the patience of concentration, the patience of wisdom, the patience of liberation, and the patience of the knowledge and vision of liberation;
by contemplating the causes and effects of the three realms, he attains the patience of emptiness, the patience of signlessness, and the patience of wishlessness;

by contemplating the impermanence of all phenomena, whether provisional or real, within the two truths, he attains the patience of impermanence; and by realizing that all phenomena are empty, he attains the patience of non-arising."
A Bodhisattva at this stage becomes a Wheel-Turning King and is able to extensively transform and benefit all sentient beings.
Furthermore, a Bodhisattva of "Patience through Faith" refers to those on the Stage of Joy,
the Stage of Purity, and the Stage of Radiance, who are able to sever the three obstructions— the bonds of form and afflictions.
They practice the four means of integration—generosity, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and cooperation;
they cultivate the four immeasurables—the immeasurable mind of loving-kindness, the immeasurable mind of compassion, the immeasurable mind of sympathetic joy, and the immeasurable mind of equanimity;

and they possess the four great vows—to sever all entanglements and hindrances, to constantly transform sentient beings, to cultivate the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and to achieve supreme enlightenment.
They abide in the three gates of liberation—the gate of emptiness, the gate of signlessness, and the gate of wishlessness.

This is the root of all practices for a bodhisattva mahāsattva, from the first generation of the mind of awakening until the attainment of omniscience, for the purpose of benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings.

"Furthermore, the Bodhisattva of Accordant Patience—namely, those in the Blazing Wisdom Ground, the Difficult to Conquer Ground, and the Manifest Ground—is able to sever the three obstructions and the bonds of mental afflictions; they can travel throughout billions of Buddha-fields in the ten directions within a single body, manifesting ineffable supernatural transformations to bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings."
"Furthermore, regarding the Bodhisattvas of the Patience of Non-arising—

namely, those on the Far-Reaching Ground, the Immovable Ground, and the Good Wisdom Ground— they are able to sever the habitual tendencies of the three obstacles within both form and mind, and can manifest unspeakable bodies to benefit all sentient beings according to their respective types."

"Furthermore, regarding the patience of quiescent extinction (*śānti-kṣānti*), both Buddhas and Bodhisattvas rely equally upon this patience. One who abides in the stage of lower patience (*adhaḥ-kṣānti*) by means of the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) is called a Bodhisattva; upon reaching the stage of higher patience (*ūrdhva-kṣānti*), one is named an Omniscient One (*sarvajña*)."
Contemplating ultimate truth and severing the marks of ignorance constitutes equal enlightenment;
this state of one mark being markless, equal and non-dual, is the eleventh stage, the Stage of All-Knowledge.

Neither existent nor non-existent, profoundly serene and pure, neither coming nor going, eternally abiding and unchanging, identical with the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and equal to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), he manifests great compassion without conditions to constantly transform sentient beings, riding the vehicle of all-knowledge to come and transform the three realms.

“Good son! All classes of sentient beings, all afflictions, the fruits of karmic maturation, and the twenty-two faculties do not transcend the three realms; this is what the Buddhas demonstrate and guide others toward.
The response-body, transformation-body, and dharma-body likewise do not depart from these.”
If anyone should say:
"Outside the three realms, there is yet another distinct realm of sentient beings," this is precisely what is taught in the *Mahābhūta-sūtra* of the non-Buddhists.
"Great King!
I have always told all sentient beings:
'One who completely cuts off and exhausts the ignorance of the three realms is called a Buddha.'"
This intrinsic purity is called the nature of original enlightenment (*mūla-avabodha*), which is the omniscient wisdom (*sarvajñajñāna*) of all Buddhas.

Because it serves as the foundation for sentient beings, it is also the basis for the practices of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; it constitutes the fourteenth of the fourteen stages of patience (*kṣānti*) within the five patiences that constitute the fundamental practice of a Bodhisattva.
The Buddha said:
"Great King!
You previously asked:..."
Regarding the question, "How does a bodhisattva transform sentient beings?"—a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should transform them in this way:

from the first stage to the final stage, because they possess all knowledge and vision regarding their own sphere of practice as well as the sphere of the Buddhas' practice. If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwells in a hundred buddha-fields, acting as a wheel-turning sage king (*cakravartin*) of Jambudvīpa, cultivates a hundred gates of illumination of the Dharma (*dharmāloka-mukha*), and dwells in a mind of equanimity through the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*), they transform all sentient beings throughout the four continents;

if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwells in a thousand buddha-fields, acting as the king of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, cultivates a thousand gates of illumination of the Dharma, and teaches the ten paths of wholesome action to transform all sentient beings.

If a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in ten thousand Buddha-fields, acts as the King of the Yāma Heaven, cultivates ten thousand gates of illumination of the Dharma, and transforms all sentient beings by relying on the four dhyānas;

if a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in one billion Buddha-fields, acts as the King of the Tuṣita Heaven, cultivates one billion gates of illumination of the Dharma, practices the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma), and transforms all sentient beings;

if a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in ten billion Buddha-fields, acts as the King of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, cultivates ten billion gates of illumination of the Dharma, and transforms all sentient beings through the two truths and the four truths.

If a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in a thousand billion Buddha-lands, acting as the King of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, he cultivates a thousand billion gates of Dharma-luminosity, using the wisdom of the twelve links of dependent origination to transform all sentient beings;

if a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in ten trillion Buddha-lands, acting as the Brahma King of the First Dhyāna, he cultivates ten trillion gates of Dharma-luminosity, using the wisdom of skillful means to transform all sentient beings;

if a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in Buddha-lands as numerous as the atoms in a million worlds, acting as the Brahma King of the Second Dhyāna, he cultivates gates of Dharma-luminosity as numerous as the atoms in a million worlds, using the wisdom of vows and supernormal powers that simultaneously illumine both [subject and object] in equality to transform all sentient beings.

If a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in as many Buddha-fields as there are atoms in ten million billion *asaṃkhyeya* worlds, acts as a Brahmā King of the Third Dhyāna, cultivates as many gates of Dharma-illumination (*dharmāloka-mukha*) as there are atoms in ten million billion *asaṃkhyeya* worlds, and transforms all sentient beings through the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge;

or if a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields, acts as a Great Brahmā King of the Fourth Dhyāna and sovereign of the triple world, cultivates unspeakably unspeakable gates of Dharma-illumination, attains the Samādhi of Ultimate Principle, shares the sphere of action of the Buddhas, exhausts the source of the triple world, and universally benefits sentient beings according to the realm of a Buddha—this is the matter of a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva manifesting the bodies of various kings to guide and transform others.
"The Tathāgatas of the ten directions are likewise; having realized unexcelled enlightenment, they constantly pervade the Dharma-realm, bringing benefit and joy to all sentient beings.
At that time, the entire great assembly rose from their seats, scattering unspeakable flowers and burning unspeakable incense, making offerings, paying homage, and praising the Tathāgata.
At that time, King Prasenajit immediately praised the Buddha before him in verse:
"The World-Honored One, the Guide, with a body of diamond, Turns the wheel of Dharma with a mind and conduct of quiescence.
With the eightfold eloquence and perfect voice, he expounds the teaching; In this assembly, hundreds of billions attain the Way."
Devas and humans together cultivate the practice of renunciation, Able to train in all the paths of the bodhisattvas;
The wondrous dharma-gate of the merits of the five patiences— Fourteen bodhisattvas were able to understand it clearly.
The three stages of worthiness and the ten levels of sagehood proceed within the practice of patience; only the Buddha alone can exhaust the source.
The Dharma, the Sangha, and the ocean-like Triple Gem—within this treasury, immeasurable merit is subsumed.
When Bodhisattvas of the ten wholesome paths resolve their great mind, they forever part from the ocean of suffering in the three realms.
Those with middling or lower grades of goodness become minor kings; those with superior grades of the ten wholesome paths become Iron-Wheel Kings.
The Seed-of-Practice stage becomes a Copper-Wheel King over two continents, while the Nature-of-Species stage becomes a Silver-Wheel King over three continents.
The Wheel-Turning King of Firm Virtue in the Path-Elements, with his seven treasures and golden wheel over the four continents;

the thirty persons of the Noble Embryo of Subduing Patience—those of the ten abodes, ten practices, and ten transferences—in whom all Buddhas of the three periods train: there are none who do not arise from this patience of subduing.
The root of all bodhisattva practices, Therefore, the arousal of the mind and the cultivation of faith are difficult.
If one attains faith, one will certainly not regress, Entering the first stage of the path of non-arising.
Bringing benefit and transformation to oneself and others equally— This is called the bodhisattva’s initial arousal of the mind.
The Bodhisattva King of the Wheel-Turning Joy, First illuminates the principle of the equality of the two truths;
Through expedient transformations, he guides sentient beings as he travels through a hundred lands, Purifying his giving of alms to benefit all living beings.
The prajñā that enters into principle is called "abiding"; the arising of virtuous conduct from this abiding is called "ground.
In the first abiding, one-mindfulness possesses all virtues, remaining unmoved within the ultimate truth.
The Bodhisattva Vigatamala, King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, manifests his form throughout the six realms and a thousand lands;
his feet of precepts are pure and perfectly complete, forever free from the faults of transgressions and errors.
Signless, objectless, and of true nature, Without substance, without birth, and illuminating non-duality;
The Bodhisattva Emitting Light, King of the Yāma Heaven, Manifests forms and proceeds to ten thousand Buddha-fields.
Skillfully penetrating samādhi, Mastery over concealment and manifestation, endowed with the three insights;
In the stages of Joy, Freedom from Defilement, and Radiance, Able to extinguish the afflictions that bind one to form;
Fully observing all actions of body and speech, The nature of phenomena is pure and its illumination is perfect.
The Bodhisattva Arciṣmatī, of great vigor, as the King of Tuṣita, wanders through billions of lands;
with the wisdom of ultimate reality and the wisdom of skillful means, he realizes the principle of non-arising and illuminates both emptiness and existence.
The Bodhisattva Sudurjaya attains equanimity, as the King of Nirmāṇarati, over billions of realms.
Contemplating with the truth of emptiness within emptiness, they perceive no dualistic marks; manifesting forms throughout the six realms of existence, there is nowhere they do not pervade.
Appearing before the Bodhisattvas as Sovereign Kings, they perceive that the characteristics of dependent origination are non-dual.
With the light of ultimate wisdom able to fill all places, they travel to thousands of billions of lands to transform sentient beings.
The stages of Blazing Wisdom, Difficult to Conquer, and Manifest Presence Can sever the delusions of the mind and the three obstructions;
With the wisdom of emptiness, tranquil and without objective conditions, They reflect back upon the infinite realm of the empty mind.
The Bodhisattva Dūraga, King of the First Dhyāna, Abides in the patience of signlessness and non-arising;
With skillful means that are entirely impartial, He constantly transforms sentient beings across ten billion lands.
Entering the stage of the stream of immovable dharma, Forever free from分段 (pariccheda) and transcending all realms of existence,
Constantly contemplating the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) and illuminating non-duality, For twenty-one births practicing in emptiness and quiescence—
The subtle ignorance (*avidyā-vāsanā*) of craving for the Dharma that accords with the Path, Only the Great Being on the Far-Reaching Stage (*dūraṃgamā*) can sever alone.
The Bodhisattva Acala, King of the Second Dhyāna, Has attained a transformation body and is eternally sovereign;
Within millions of lands as numerous as motes of dust, He transforms sentient beings according to their various forms.
He fully knows the immeasurable kalpas of the three periods of time, Yet remains unmoved within the ultimate truth.
The Bodhisattva Good Wisdom, King of the Third Dhyāna, Can manifest [himself] simultaneously throughout a thousand Ganges-sands of worlds;
Ever abiding in the practice of unconditioned emptiness and stillness, He fully realizes the treasury of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in a single thought-moment.
The Bodhisattva Dharmamegha, King of the Fourth Dhyāna, transforms sentient beings across billions of Ganges-sands of lands;
having first entered the Diamond-like Samādhi where all is fully realized, he has forever transcended twenty-nine births.
Within the patience of cessation (*śānti-kṣānti*), he contemplates the lower patience (*mṛdu-kṣānti*); with a single turn, he attains the wondrous enlightenment that is peerless.
The Immovable, Good Wisdom, and Dharma Cloud stages eliminate all prior habitual tendencies of ignorance;
as these tendencies and their associated consciousnesses cease to function together, the principles of the two truths are perfected without exception.
Perfectly awakened, signless, pervading the Dharma-realm, The wisdom of the exhaustion of the thirty births is perfectly luminous;
Tranquil illumination, unconditioned, true liberation— Great compassion manifests in response, peerless and equal to none.
Serenely unmoving, eternally peaceful and secure, Its radiance shines everywhere, yet there is nothing to be shone upon.
The three classes of worthies and the ten stages of sages abide in the retribution of their fruits; Only the Buddha alone dwells in the Pure Land.
All sentient beings dwell there only temporarily; Upon ascending the Diamond Ground, they are forever immovable.
The Tathāgata’s virtues of the three karmas are immeasurable; He extends equal compassion to all sentient beings.
The Dharma King, the unsurpassed tree among men, universally shades the great assembly with immeasurable light;
his mouth constantly preaches the Dharma, never without meaning, while his mind and wisdom are in tranquil extinction, illuminating without conditions.
The Lion among Men has expounded for us Profound words and meanings never before heard;
Dust-mote-like lands have all been shaken, And the great assembly, filled with joy, has all received benefit.
The World-Honored One has skillfully taught the fourteen kings; Therefore, I now prostrate myself at his feet.

At that time, a great assembly as numerous as the sands of ten million billion Ganges Rivers, having heard the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and King Prasenajit speak of the immeasurable merits of the fourteen kinds of patience, attained the great benefit of the Dharma; through hearing and understanding the Dharma, they realized the patience of non-arising and entered the stage of certainty.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly, saying:
"This King Prasenajit was already a Bodhisattva of the fourth stage during the Dharma of King Dragon-Radiance (Nāgaprabhāsa) ten thousand kalpas ago, while I was a Bodhisattva of the eighth stage;
now he utters a great lion’s roar before me."
"So it is, so it is! It is just as you have said.
The attainment of the true meaning is inconceivable; only a Buddha and a Buddha can know this matter."
“Good son! These fourteen kinds of patience, the Dharma-body of all Buddhas, and the practices of all Bodhisattvas are inconceivable and immeasurable.”
Why is this? All Buddhas are born from within the *prajñāpāramitā*, transformed within the *prajñāpāramitā*, and pass away within the *prajñāpāramitā*;
yet in reality, for all Buddhas, there is no place of birth, no place of transformation, and no place of cessation.
It is foremost and non-dual; it is neither with marks nor without marks; it has no self and no other; it neither comes nor goes, for it is like empty space. "Good son!

All sentient beings are by nature without birth or extinction; they exist as illusory transformations produced by the gathering of all phenomena. The characteristics of the aggregates, sense bases, and elements neither combine nor disperse, for phenomena are identical to the dharma-nature, being quiescent and empty.
All sentient beings are pure by nature; the various practices they perform are neither bound nor liberated, being neither cause nor effect, yet not without cause or effect.
This is because all suffering, feelings, practices, afflictions, the marks of self and person, and the knower, the seer, and the recipient are entirely empty.

The realm of phenomena is empty; it is empty, signless, and wishless. It does not conform to perversions nor to illusory transformations. It has no marks of the six destinies, no marks of the four modes of birth, no marks of noble beings, and no marks of the Three Jewels, for it is like space.

“Good son! The profound *prajñā* is without knowing and without seeing; it does not function and does not take objects; it neither abandons nor receives. It dwells correctly in observation without the appearance of signs, for one who practices this path is like space.”
The characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) are such that both the mind that perceives attainment and the mind that perceives non-attainment are unobtainable.

Therefore, Prajñā is neither identical to the five aggregates nor separate from the five aggregates; it is neither identical to sentient beings nor separate from sentient beings; it is neither identical to objects of perception nor separate from objects of perception; it is neither identical to practice and understanding nor separate from practice and understanding. Such characteristics as these are inconceivable.

Therefore, all the practices cultivated by Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are carried out while they have not yet reached the ultimate; all Buddhas know these to be like illusions and transformations, and having attained the mark of non-abiding, they transform within them. Thus, the fourteen kinds of patience are inconceivable.
“Good son! This treasury of merit that you have now described brings great benefit to all sentient beings.

Even if bodhisattvas of the tenth stage were as numerous as the sands of immeasurable Ganges Rivers to speak of this merit, it would be but a single drop in an ocean compared to its hundred thousand billion parts. The Buddhas of the three periods of time know it as it truly is, and all worthy sages praise it; therefore, I shall now briefly describe a small portion of the merit you have spoken of.”

“Good son! These fourteen patiences have been practiced by all bodhisattvas of the past and present throughout the worlds of the ten directions, and have been revealed by all buddhas; future buddhas and bodhisattva-mahāsattvas shall do likewise.”
If Buddhas and Bodhisattvas were to attain all-knowledge by means other than this gateway, such a thing is impossible.
Why? Because there is no alternative path for the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

“Good son! If there is a person who, upon hearing of these patiences—namely, the patience of abiding, the patience of practice, the patience of dedication, the patience of joy, the patience of freedom from defilement, the patience of radiant light, the patience of flaming wisdom, the patience of difficult victory, the patience of manifestation, the patience of far-reaching travel, the patience of immovability, the patience of excellent wisdom, the patience of the dharma-cloud, and the patience of perfect enlightenment—is able to give rise to even a single thought of pure faith, that person shall transcend all sufferings and difficulties for hundreds of kalpas, thousands of kalpas, and immeasurable, boundless kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. They shall not be born in the evil realms and shall before long attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”

At that time, ten billion Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas named Ākāśagarbha, together with an immeasurable and incalculable assembly of those who had gathered, leaped for joy and, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, saw throughout the ten directions Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, each at their respective sites of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) preaching the fourteen kinds of patience (*kṣānti*). These were no different from what our World-Honored One had taught; each was filled with joy and practiced the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) exactly as it had been explained.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed King Prasenajit:
"You previously asked:
'Furthermore, by what characteristic does one abide in observation?'"
"A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should contemplate in this way:
seeing the illusory transformation with an illusory body, they abide correctly in equanimity, free from the distinction of self and other.

Observing in this manner, they transform and benefit sentient beings; yet, throughout kalpas of long antiquity, the initial momentary consciousness of all sentient beings differs from wood or stone, and through birth, it acquires both defilement and purity, each acting as the basis for immeasurable and innumerable defiled and pure consciousnesses."

From the first moment of an unspeakable number of kalpas until the final moment of the vajra-like state, there exist unspeakably unspeakable numbers of consciousnesses that give rise to the two dharmas of sentient beings—form and mind: form being called the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), and mind being called the four aggregates (*catur-skandha*). These are all of a cumulative nature and conceal the ultimate reality.

“Great King! This single dharma of form gives rise to immeasurable forms: what is apprehended by the eye is form; what is apprehended by the ear is sound; what is apprehended by the nose is fragrance; what is apprehended by the tongue is taste; what is apprehended by the body is tangibility; that which is firm and stable is called earth;
that which is moist and fluid is called water; that whose nature is warmth is called fire; and that which is light and mobile is called wind.”
The places where the five consciousnesses arise are called the five material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*).
In this manner, through successive transformation, from a single form and a single mind, there arise unspeakably infinite forms and minds, all of which are like illusions.
“Good son! The sensations of sentient beings are established based on worldly convention as either existent or non-existent.
However, it is merely the arising of conceptualizations and recollections in sentient beings that they perform actions and experience their fruits; all such things are termed conventional truth.”

All sentient beings within the three realms and six destinies—whether Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras—as well as the notions of self and person, and all phenomena of form and mind, are like what is seen in a dream.
"Good son! All names are merely provisional designations.
Before the Buddha appeared in the world, within the illusory phenomena of conventional truth, there were no names, no meanings, and no essential characteristics."
There are no names for the three realms, nor names for the good and evil karmic retributions of the six destinies;
yet, when the Buddhas appear, for the sake of sentient beings, they speak of the immeasurable names of the three realms, the six destinies, and defilement and purity.

All these things are like echoes; the continuity of all phenomena does not abide for even a single moment. From instant to instant, they are neither identical nor different; arising and ceasing rapidly, they are neither annihilated nor eternal, for all conditioned phenomena are like a mirage. All phenomena exist in mutual dependence—namely, the form-element, the eye-element, and the eye-consciousness-element, up to the dharma-element, the mind-element, and the mind-consciousness-element—which, like a flash of lightning, depend on one another without fixed certainty. Their existence, non-existence, identity, or difference is like a second moon; all phenomena are produced through conditions.
The phenomena of the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) are like bubbles upon water; all phenomena are produced through causes.
For all sentient beings, simultaneous causes and effects, as well as sequential causes and effects, and the good and evil of the three periods of time are like clouds in the sky. "Good son!

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in non-discrimination; he is without the marks of 'this' and 'that,' and without the marks of 'self' and 'other,' constantly practicing the benefit and transformation of others without the mark of benefiting or transforming."
Therefore, one should know that the defiled consciousness of the foolish is bound by the signs of attachment to the unreal;

whereas the Bodhisattva, through clear vision, knows it to be like a phantom person, devoid of intrinsic nature or characteristics, being merely like a flower in the sky. This is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s dwelling in the benefit of self and others through suchness-contemplation.

When this Dharma was being taught, among the immeasurable assembly of humans and devas, there were those who attained the Patience of Subjugation (kṣānti), the Patience of Emptiness and Non-arising (śūnyatā-anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), and the first through the tenth stages (bhūmi). Furthermore, immeasurable Bodhisattvas attained the stage of being born only once more before reaching Buddhahood (ekajātipratibaddha).
At that time, King Prasenajit addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Is there conventional truth within ultimate truth?”
If one says it does not exist, wisdom should not be dualistic;
if one says it exists,
wisdom should not be unitary.
"What is the meaning of 'one and two,' and what are its matters?
The Buddha said,
"Great King!"

"In the past, within the Dharma of King Dragon-Radiance Buddha, you already asked about this meaning; now I have nothing to say, and you have nothing to hear. This absence of speaking and hearing is precisely what is called 'one meaning' and 'two meanings.'"
"Listen attentively now; I shall speak for you.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The signless ultimate truth, Its essence is not created by itself or by another."
Conditioned phenomena exist like illusions, Nor are they created by self or another.
The nature of dharmas is fundamentally without nature;
In the ultimate truth, they are empty and such-like.
All phenomena that exist as illusions exist through the collection of the three types of conventional designations;
they do not exist as ultimate reality, for they are empty in the sense of the sublime truth of cessation.
All phenomena exist through causes and conditions; such is the meaning of existence and non-existence.
Existence and non-existence are fundamentally dual, like the two horns of an ox;
yet when illuminated by understanding, they are seen to be non-dual. Thus, the two truths are eternally not identical.
Understanding the mind sees that there is no duality; though one seeks duality, it cannot be found.
It is not said that the two truths are one, yet even oneness cannot be found.
In understanding, there is always inherent unity; in the truths, there is always inherent duality.
To thoroughly comprehend these two truths is to truly enter the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
Conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) arises as an illusion, like flowers in the sky, like shadows, or like the optical illusion of falling hairs; it exists as a phantom due to causes and conditions.
Seeing an illusion as an illusion, the fool calls it a "real illusion";
seeing illusory phenomena, the magician knows that both reality and illusion are entirely non-existent.
If one understands these dharmas in this way, one will comprehend the meaning of both unity and duality.
Regarding all phenomena, one should contemplate them in this way:
"Great King!
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas dwell in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) to transform sentient beings, the Buddha and sentient beings are one and not two."
Why is this? Both sentient beings and bodhi are empty.

Because sentient beings are empty, one can establish the emptiness of bodhi; because bodhi is empty, one can establish the emptiness of sentient beings. This is because all phenomena are empty through the emptiness of emptiness.

Why is this? Because Prajñā is signless and both truths are empty; that is to say, from ignorance up to all-knowledge, there is no self-characteristic and no other-characteristic. Within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), one sees nothing to be seen. Whether one practices or does not practice, one does not grasp at them; whether it is practicing or not practicing, one does not grasp at them; nor does one grasp at neither practicing nor not practicing. One does not grasp at any phenomena whatsoever.
When a bodhisattva has not yet attained Buddhahood, they take awakening (bodhi) to be affliction;
when a bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, they take affliction to be awakening. Why is this?
"Because in the ultimate sense there is no duality, all Buddhas, Tathāgatas, and all phenomena are entirely suchness.
King Prasenajit addressed the Buddha, saying,
"How is it that the Buddhas of the ten directions and all Bodhisattvas practice the true reality without departing from words and letters?"
The Buddha said:
"Great King!

As for 'letters,' they refer to the sūtras, geyas, vyākaraṇas, gāthās, udānas, nidānas, avadānas, itivṛttakas, jātaka, vaipulya, adbhutadharmas, and upadeśas. All the sounds, speech, letters, and phrases therein that are proclaimed are all suchness; there is nothing that is not the true mark."
If one grasps at the characteristics of words and letters, that is not the true characteristic.
"Great King!
One who cultivates the true characteristic cultivates it in the same manner as words and letters."

The true mark (*dharmatā*) is the mother of the wisdom of all Buddhas and the fundamental mother of wisdom for all sentient beings; this is precisely what is called the essence of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
When Buddhas have not yet attained Buddhahood, it serves as the mother of wisdom for those future Buddhas;
once Buddhas have already attained Buddhahood, it becomes their omniscience itself.
That which has not yet been attained is its nature; that which has already been attained is wisdom.
The Prajñā of the Three Vehicles is neither born nor extinguished; its self-nature is eternally abiding.
For all sentient beings, this is their enlightened nature.

If a bodhisattva neither clings to words nor departs from words, having no characteristic of words yet not being without words, and can practice in this way without perceiving the characteristic of practice, this is called one who practices with words; such a person is able to attain the true nature of prajñā, which is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
“Great King!
It is in this way that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva protects the fruit of Buddhahood, protects the practices of the ten stages, and protects the transformation of sentient beings.
King Prasenajit addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The true nature is one, yet the faculties, behaviors, and categories of sentient beings are immeasurable. Is the Dharma-gate one, or is it immeasurable?
The Buddha said, “Great King!...”
The Dharma-gates are neither one nor are they infinite.

Why is this? Because the physical and mental phenomena of sentient beings, the characteristics of the five aggregates of clinging, and their various faculties, conducts, and categories—such as notions of self, person, and cognitive views—are boundless; accordingly, the Dharma-gates are also infinite in accordance with those faculties.
The nature of these phenomena is neither with marks nor without marks, yet it is not without measure.

If a bodhisattva, following the perceptions of sentient beings, perceives one or perceives two, this is precisely not seeing the meaning of one or two—knowing that one and two are neither one nor two is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*);
grasping at one and two as being either existent or non-existent is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Therefore, this dharma-gate is neither one nor two.
“Great King!
All Buddhas have taught the Prajñāpāramitā; I now teach the Prajñāpāramitā as being non-dual and without distinction.”
"You great assembly, by upholding, reciting, and practicing according to these teachings as they were spoken, you will thereby uphold the Dharma of all Buddhas. Great King!

The merit of this Prajñāpāramitā is immeasurable. Suppose there were as many unspeakably numerous Buddhas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, and each one of those Buddhas were to convert unspeakably numerous sentient beings, and each of those sentient beings were to attain Buddhahood; and suppose those Buddhas, in turn, were to convert unspeakably numerous sentient beings, who likewise all attained Buddhahood; and suppose all those Buddhas were to speak the Prajñāpāramitā in unspeakably numerous nayutas of billions of verses—it could never be fully recounted."

If one were to take a single verse from among all these verses and divide it into a thousand parts, and then explain only one part of those thousand parts, the merit of its words and meaning would still be inexhaustible; how much more so, then, the merit inherent in all such immeasurable words and meanings!

If there is anyone who can give rise to even a single thought of pure faith in this sutra, that person will immediately transcend the sufferings of birth and death for hundreds of kalpas, thousands of kalpas, and hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas; how much more so for those who copy, receive and uphold, read and recite, or explain it to others—the merit they obtain is equal to that of all Buddhas of the ten directions, without any difference.
"You should know that this person is protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas and will before long attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.

When this Dharma was spoken, one billion people attained the patience of the three emptinesses (*trīṇi śūnyatā-kṣāntayaḥ*), ten trillion people attained the patience of great emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā-kṣānti*), and immeasurable Bodhisattvas attained the stage of the tenth ground (*daśabhūmi*).
The Benevolent Kings’ Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra for the Protection of the State, Volume I;
The Benevolent Kings’ Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra for the Protection of the State, Volume II.
By the Duke of Su, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, with the Rank of Grand Marshal and Peer of the Three Ducal Princes.
Feudal fief of three thousand households; conferred the rank of *sī* (Purple Robe); posthumously granted the title of Minister of Works (*Sīkōng*); posthumous name: Dàjiàn (Great Mirror).

Translated by the Tripitaka Śramaṇa Amoghavajra of Dàguǎngzhì Dàxīngshàn Monastery, by Imperial Decree. Chapter Five: Protecting the State At that time, the World-Honored One addressed King Prasenajit and the other great kings:
"Listen attentively! Listen attentively!"
I shall explain for you the Dharma for protecting the state.
When all lands are about to fall into chaos, and when various calamities arise and bandits come to destroy them, you kings should receive, uphold, read, and recite this Prajñāpāramitā;

you should adorn the site of practice (maṇḍala), place one hundred Buddha images, one hundred Bodhisattva images, and one hundred lion thrones there, and invite one hundred Dharma masters to expound this sūtra.

Before each seat, they shall light various lamps, burn various incenses, and scatter various flowers, making vast offerings of clothing, bedding, food and drink, medicinal decoctions, dwellings, and couches— providing all manner of service—
and recite and study this sutra twice every day.

If kings, ministers, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās listen to and receive it, read and recite it, and practice according to the Dharma, all calamities and disasters will immediately be extinguished.
"Great King!
Within these various lands there are immeasurable spirits and ghosts, each with their own immeasurable retinues; if they hear this sutra, they will protect your kingdom."
If a state is about to fall into chaos, the ghosts and spirits will first become disordered;
because the ghosts and spirits are disordered, the myriad people will likewise fall into chaos—thieves will arise and the common people will perish;
the king, the crown prince, the princes, and the hundred officials will engage in mutual accusations and disputes.

When heaven and earth undergo strange transformations, and the sun, moon, and myriad stars lose their proper seasons and orbits; when great fires, great floods, and great winds arise—when such calamities occur, one should in every case uphold and expound this Prajñāpāramitā.

If one receives, upholds, reads, and recites this sutra, all that is sought—official rank, wealth and abundance, sons and daughters, wisdom and understanding, the ability to travel wherever one desires, and the karmic rewards of human and celestial realms—all shall be fully attained;
epidemics and calamities shall be immediately cured;
and those whose bodies are bound by shackles, fetters, cangues, and locks shall all obtain liberation.
"Violations of the four grave precepts, the commission of the five heinous crimes, and the destruction of all other precepts—all such immeasurable transgressions shall be completely extinguished.
Great King!
In the distant past, Śakra Devānām Indra was King Mūrdhaja; leading the fourfold army, he came to the celestial palace with the intent to destroy Śakra."
Then that Lord of Devas, in accordance with the teachings of all past Buddhas, prepared one hundred high seats and invited one hundred Dharma masters to lecture and recite the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra.
Māndhātṛ immediately descended, and the celestial hosts were at peace.
"Great King!

Formerly, King Tālajaṅgha had a crown prince named Pāda-lekhana. When he ascended the throne, there was a non-Buddhist teacher named Kalyāṇadatta who performed the consecration for him, commanding Pāda-lekhana to take the heads of a thousand kings to offer as sacrifice to Mahākāla, the great black deity of the charnel grounds."
Since ascending the throne, he has already obtained nine hundred and ninety-nine kings, lacking only one.
Traveling ten thousand li to the north, he finally found a king named Puming (Universal Radiance).
The King Samantaprabha said to Pāṇḍupāda,
"I pray that you will grant me one day to pay homage to the Triple Gem and provide food for the śramaṇas.
Having heard this, Pāṇḍupāda immediately granted his permission.

The king, following the teachings spoken by the Buddhas of the past, prepared one hundred high seats and invited one hundred Dharma masters to lecture on the eight billion verses of the *Prajñāpāramitā* twice each day.
Then, the foremost Dharma Master among that assembly spoke a verse for King Samantaprabha:
"The kalpa-fire blazes forth, and the great trichiliocosm is utterly destroyed; Mount Sumeru and the vast oceans are consumed until nothing remains."
Even the Brahmās, Śakras, devas, nāgas, and all other sentient beings shall eventually perish; how much more so this body?
Birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction—pressed upon by enemies and kin alike—can thwart even one’s wishes.
The fetters and latent tendencies of craving create one's own sores and ulcers; there is no peace in the three realms—what joy can there be in a kingdom?
Conditioned things are unreal, arising from causes and conditions; like lightning, they flash with prosperity and decline, existing for a moment and then vanishing.
The various realms, destinies, and births appear according to the conditions of karma; they are like shadows and echoes—all are empty.
Consciousness is driven by karma and arises dependent upon the four great elements; bound by ignorance and craving, the notions of "self" and "mine" arise.
"Consciousness migrates according to karma, and the body has no master;
one should know that the realm of the land is likewise a phantom transformation.

When the Dharma Master had spoken this verse, King Samantaprabha heard the Dharma and attained realization, realizing the Samādhi of Emptiness, while the king’s retinue attained the emptiness of the Dharma-eye.
The king immediately went to the kingdom of Tāla and, in the midst of the assembly of kings, spoke these words:
"O virtuous ones!
The time for my life to end has now arrived."
"You should all recite and uphold the verses on the Prajñāpāramitā spoken by the Buddhas of the past.
Upon hearing this, the kings also attained awakening and understanding; they realized the samādhi of emptiness and each began to recite and uphold them.
At that time, King Pādapāṇi asked the kings, "What teachings are you all currently reciting?

Then, Samantaprabha immediately answered King Pādapāṇi with the aforementioned verses. Upon hearing this Dharma, the king also realized the samādhi of emptiness; filled with joy and leaping for gladness, he addressed the kings, saying:
"I have been misled by the false teachers of external paths; this is not your fault.
Each of you should return to your respective countries and invite a Dharma Master to explain the Prajñāpāramitā."

"At that time, King Pādapāṇi entrusted the kingdom to his younger brother and left the household life to practice the Way, attaining the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
'Great King!
In the past, there were furthermore five thousand kings who constantly recited this sutra and obtained its retribution in their present lives.'"
You sixteen great kings, who practice the Dharma for protecting the state, should likewise uphold, recite, and explain this sutra;
furthermore, any kings in future ages who wish to protect their nations and themselves should also likewise uphold, recite, and explain this sutra.

When this Dharma was being taught, immeasurable multitudes attained the stage of non-retrogression; the asuras and others were reborn in the heavens; and immeasurable, incalculable devas of the desire and form realms attained the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharmakṣānti).

At that time, the sixteen kings and the great assembly, having heard the Buddha expound these profound words and meanings of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, were filled with joy and leaped for gladness. They scattered hundreds of billions of precious lotus flowers, which formed a jeweled flower throne in mid-air;
upon this throne, the immeasurable assemblies of the Buddhas of the ten directions sat together and preached the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
This great assembly took ten thousand golden lotus flowers and scattered them over Śākyamuni Buddha; they merged together to form a floral canopy that covered the entire assembly.

They further scattered eighty-four thousand *puṇḍarīka* flowers, which formed a white cloud-palace in the void. Within this palace, King of Radiance Buddha, together with the Buddhas of the ten directions and an immeasurable great assembly, expounded the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
This great assembly took hold of *mandārava* flowers and scattered them over Śākyamuni Buddha and the entire congregation;

they further scattered *mañjūṣaka* flowers, which transformed in mid-air into a precious city of vajra. Within that city, the Buddha Siṃhavikrīḍitarāja, together with the Buddhas of the ten directions and the multitude of great bodhisattvas, expounded the ultimate Prajñāpāramitā.

Furthermore, they scattered immeasurable, exquisite celestial flowers, which formed precious cloud-canopies in the void, covering the entire trichiliocosm; from within these flower canopies, flowers as numerous as the sands of the Ganges rained down from the sky.
At that time, King Prasenajit and the great assembly, having witnessed this event, marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence. Joining their palms toward the Buddha, they spoke these words:
“May all Buddhas of the past, present, and future always preach the Prajñāpāramitā;
may all sentient beings always be able to see and hear it, no different from ourselves today.”
The Buddha said,
"Great King, it is as you have said."

This Prajñāpāramitā is the mother of all Buddhas and the mother of all Bodhisattvas; it is the source from which uncommon merits and supernormal powers arise. All Buddhas alike proclaim that it brings great benefit; therefore, you should always uphold and maintain it.

At that time, the World-Honored One manifested inconceivable supernatural transformations for the great assembly: a single flower entered into immeasurable flowers, and immeasurable flowers entered into a single flower;
a single buddha-field entered into immeasurable buddha-fields, and immeasurable buddha-fields entered into a single buddha-field;
a single atom-sized world-system entered into immeasurable atom-sized world-systems, and immeasurable atom-sized world-systems entered into a single atom-sized world-system.
Immeasurable great oceans enter into a single pore;
immeasurable Mount Sumerus enter into a mustard seed;
the body of a single Buddha enters the bodies of immeasurable sentient beings, and the bodies of immeasurable sentient beings enter the body of a single Buddha.
The great manifests as small, and the small manifests as great;
the pure manifests as defiled, and the defiled manifests as pure.
The body of the Buddha is inconceivable, the bodies of sentient beings are inconceivable, and even the worlds are inconceivable.

When the Buddha manifested this supernatural transformation, ten thousand women transformed their female bodies and attained the samādhi of supernormal powers; immeasurable devas and humans attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); immeasurable asuras and others established themselves on the path of bodhisattvas; and bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges manifested their bodies as Buddhas.

At that time, King Prasenajit beheld the Buddha’s miraculous transformation—seeing the Tathāgata Samantaprabha upon the thousand-petaled lotus pedestal, the thousand transformation Buddhas upon the thousand petals, and the immeasurable Buddhas within each petal, each preaching the Prajñāpāramitā—and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!...”
Such immeasurable *prajñāpāramitā* cannot be known by consciousness nor understood by wisdom.
How, then, can these sons of good family clearly comprehend and awaken to this sūtra, and expound it for others?
The Buddha said:
"Great King!
Listen attentively now!"

From the initial cultivation of patience up to the Vajra-samādhi, the practice of the thirteen gates of contemplation according to the Dharma serves as the support and foundation for the Dharma Master.
You, the great assembly, should honor him as you would the Buddha, presenting him with hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of celestial, exquisite incenses and flowers.

“Good son! That Dharma-preacher is a Bodhisattva of the nature of the stage of practice (śikṣā-bhūmi). Whether as a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, upāsaka, or upāsikā, they cultivate the ten stages of practice; they see the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha and resolve upon bodhicitta; they feel compassion for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings; they personally contemplate their own body’s six elements and faculties as entirely impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self; they thoroughly understand karmic actions, birth-and-death, and nirvāṇa; and they are able to benefit themselves and others, providing them with profit, peace, and happiness—whether hearing praise or disparagement of the Buddha, their mind remains steadfast and unmoved; whether hearing that there is a Buddha or that there is no Buddha, their mind remains steadfast and does not regress.”

With no lapses in the three types of action, they give rise to the six points of harmonious respect; through skillful means, they discipline sentient beings; they diligently study the ten knowledges and supernatural powers for the sake of transformation and benefit; and they practice the eighty-four thousand pāramitās at the lower level.

“Good son! Prior to the stage of practicing patience (kṣānti), for ten thousand kalpas, one practices the ten wholesome actions with both regression and progress, like light feathers drifting east and west with the wind.”

If one reaches the stage of patience (*kṣānti*), one enters the assembly of those fixed in rightness (*samyaktva-niyāma*); because one does not commit the five heinous crimes nor slander the true Dharma, and because one knows that the characteristics of my dharmas are entirely empty, one abides in the stage of liberation.

By practicing this patience for one asaṃkhyeya kalpa, one is able to give rise to superior conduct. Furthermore, the bodhisattva of the nature-lineage dwells in non-conceptualization and cultivates the ten wisdom-observations:

because he relinquishes wealth and life; because he maintains pure precepts; because his mind is humble; because he benefits himself and others; because he is undisturbed by birth and death; because he is signless and profoundly deep; because he realizes existence is like an illusion; because he does not seek karmic retribution; because he attains the unimpeded analytical knowledges; and because he manifests the spiritual powers of a Buddha in every thought-moment. He counteracts the four inversions, the three unwholesome roots, the delusions and karma of the three periods of time, and the ten perversions. Realizing that the views of self and person are false in every thought-moment, he thoroughly understands that the designation of names, the designation of experience, and the designation of phenomena are all unobtainable. Being free from the marks of self and other, he dwells in the observation of reality.

In the intermediate stage of cultivation, one practices eighty-four thousand pāramitās for two asaṃkhyeya kalpas, performing various sublime deeds and attaining the stage of steadfast endurance (kṣānti).

"Furthermore, a Bodhisattva of the lineage of the path (mārga-gotraka) dwells within steadfast patience (*kṣānti*) and contemplates the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*), attaining non-arising and non-ceasing. The four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*) are able to destroy all darkness; he constantly beholds the Buddhas and extensively offers them worship. He constantly studies the Buddhas and abides in the mind of dedication (*pariṇāmanā-citta*). All the roots of goodness (*kuśala-mūla*) he cultivates are identical to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). He is able to perform extensive Buddha-works within samādhi, manifesting various bodies and practicing the four methods of attraction (*catvāri saṃgraha-vastūni*). Abiding in non-discrimination, he transforms and benefits sentient beings; his wisdom is clear and penetrating, observing with profound insight. He universally cultivates all practices and vows, acting as a Dharma-master to guide and subdue sentient beings. He skillfully contemplates the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the three realms (*tridhātu*), and the two truths (*dvaya-satya*), being free from the notions of self and other, and attaining the nature of suchness (*tathatā*)."
Although they constantly cultivate the ultimate truth, they take birth within the three realms.
Why is this? Because the habitual tendencies of karma and their retributive fruits have not yet been exhausted; thus, they are born in accordance with the Path among humans and devas.

One cultivates the eighty-four thousand pāramitās of the superior grade; for three asaṃkhyeya kalpas, one practices the two types of beneficial conduct, bringing vast benefit to others, attaining well-tamed samādhis, abiding in sublime observation, and cultivating the practice of renunciation, thereby being able to realize the level of the noble ones of equality.

"Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva of the Stage of Joy (Pramuditā-bhūmi) transcends the stage of ordinary beings, is born into the family of the Tathāgatas, and dwells in the patience of equanimity (*samatā-kṣānti*).

Initially, the wisdom of signlessness (*animitta-jñāna*) illuminates the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); it is the equality of the single characteristic, being neither characterized nor signless. Having severed all ignorance and extinguished the craving of the triple world, because future immeasurable births and deaths will never again arise, he takes great compassion as his foremost priority and gives rise to various great vows. Within the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*), he moment by moment cultivates immeasurable supreme practices—neither realizing nor not realizing, because he universally studies everything;
neither dwelling nor not dwelling, because he is directed toward all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*)."
They traverse the cycle of birth and death because demons cannot move them;
they are free from the notions of "self" and "mine" because they have no fear;
and they lack the distinction between self and other because they constantly transform sentient beings.
By the power of sovereign vows, one is born in all pure lands. Good son!

This initial awakening-wisdom is neither like-ness nor wisdom; it is neither existent nor non-existent. It is free from the two marks and possesses the wondrous function of skillful means; it is neither inverted nor abiding, neither moving nor still. It is sovereign in benefiting both self and others, just as water and waves are neither identical nor different. Wisdom gives rise to the various pāramitās, which likewise are neither identical nor different.

Throughout four asaṃkhyeya kalpas, they fully cultivate and practice a million vows and practices; at this stage, the bodhisattva is free from the karmic habits of the three realms and no longer creates new karma.

By virtue of following their power of wisdom and through birth by means of aspiration, they constantly practice the perfection of generosity (dāna-pāramitā) in every thought-moment; through giving, kind speech, purposeful action, and cooperation, they are vast and pure, skillfully abiding in the benefit of sentient beings.

"Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva on the Ground of Freedom from Defilement (Vimalā) attains the most supreme tranquility of the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*).
