Having severed the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of anger and the like, they cultivate all practices, namely: being far removed from killing, not taking what is not given, and having no defiled desire in the mind; attaining speech that is truthful, harmonious, gentle, and disciplined; constantly practicing equanimity, constantly giving rise to loving-kindness, and abiding in an upright mind; being tranquil and purely wholesome, free from the defilement of breaking precepts, and maintaining the contemplation of great compassion (*mahāmaitrī*) so that it manifests in every thought-moment."
Throughout five *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, he fulfills the perfection of pure ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*), his resolve being courageous and forever free from all defilements.

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva on the Radiant Ground (*prabhākari-bhūmi*) dwells in non-conceptuality, extinguishing the darkness of ignorance; he attains the three types of higher knowledge (*vidyā*) within the patient acceptance of the signless (*animitta-kṣānti*), fully knowing that the three periods of time neither come nor go.

Relying upon the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), he accords with non-conceptual wisdom in successive stages and fulfills supreme meditative concentration. He acquires the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*): manifesting his body in various sizes with mastery over concealment and appearance; with the purity of the divine eye, he sees all realms of existence; with the purity of the divine ear, he hears all sounds; with the knowledge of others' minds, he knows the thoughts of sentient beings; and through the recollection of past lives, he can know their infinite distinctions.
Throughout six *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, he practices the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) in its entirety, attaining great dhāraṇīs that bring benefit and peace.

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva on the Ground of Blazing Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*) cultivates the conforming patience (*anulomikī-kṣānti*), remaining without grasping, because he has forever severed even the subtle views of self and phenomena (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*). He practices and masters the boundless factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*)—the foundations of mindfulness, right efforts, bases of power, faculties, powers, and limbs of awakening—in order to accomplish the powers, the fearlessnesses, and the unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*).
Throughout seven *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, he cultivated the immeasurable perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*), remained far removed from indolence, and universally benefited all sentient beings.

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva on the Ground Difficult to Conquer (*Sudurjayā-bhūmi*) accords with True Suchness (*tathatā*) by means of the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*). With a pure, equal, and non-differentiated mark, he abandons the pursuit of nirvana characteristic of the Lesser Vehicle and accumulates all merits while fully contemplating the truths: namely, the Noble Truth of Suffering, the Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path;
as well as the conventional and ultimate truths—thus contemplating immeasurable truths.

For the benefit of sentient beings, they practice all arts and crafts—writing, medicine, chanting, comedy, technical skills, incantations, and the heterodox doctrines of outsiders—ensuring there is not a single error in their knowledge of auspicious and inauspicious signs. Yet, provided these do not cause harm or distress to sentient beings, they reveal them all for the sake of benefiting others, gradually leading them to dwell securely in unsurpassed bodhi, and enabling them to know the paths that lead out of and the obstacles within the various stages (*bhūmi*).
Throughout eight asaṃkhyeya kalpas, he constantly cultivated samādhi and brought forth all practices.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva on the Ground of Presence attains the superior conformative patience (anulomikī kṣānti) and dwells in the three gates of liberation.
He is able to exhaust the causes and karmic accumulations that give rise to the three realms, as well as their coarse manifestations.
With great compassion as his primary motivation, he contemplates all births and deaths:

obscured by the darkness of ignorance, the seeds of consciousness accumulate karma; thus, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age and death all arise from attachment to a self.
Ignorance, karma, and their fruits are neither existent nor non-existent, for they are of one mark and markless, being non-dual.
Throughout nine asaṃkhyeya kalpas, he practiced a million samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, thereby attaining the boundless illumination of all Prajñāpāramitā.

"Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva on the Ground of Far-Reaching cultivates the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and realizes the non-distinction of phenomena. He severs the subtle manifestations of all karmic fruits, dwells in the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), and gives rise to extraordinary practices. Although he is eternally quiescent, he extensively transforms sentient beings—manifesting entry among the Śrāvakas while constantly following the Buddha’s wisdom;
manifesting as being identical to non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*); and manifesting as a Māra king, conforming to the world while remaining eternally transcendent."

Throughout ten asaṃkhyeya kalpas, he practiced a million samādhis; through skillful means, he extensively proclaimed the treasury of the Dharma, and all adornments were brought to complete perfection.

"Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva of the Immovable Ground abides in the patience of non-arising; his essence is without increase or decrease, he has severed all functional efforts, and his mind-moments are quiescent, being devoid of the characteristics of body or mind, like empty space."

This Bodhisattva does not give rise to thoughts of Buddhahood, bodhicitta, or nirvana; yet, by virtue of their original vows and through the empowerment of all Buddhas, they are able, in a single moment of thought, to initiate the activity of wisdom that simultaneously illuminates both [the conventional and the ultimate] in equality. With the wisdom of the ten powers, they pervade unspeakably many great trichiliocosms, universally bringing benefit and happiness to all sentient beings according to their needs.
Throughout a thousand *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, they fulfill a million great vows, and with every thought-moment, they enter into all modes and the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva on the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*Sādhumatī-bhūmi*) dwells in the supreme patience regarding non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), extinguishes the characteristics of the mind and mental states, realizes mastery over wisdom, severs the obstacles of hindrance, and possesses great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). Having cultivated the powers and fearlessnesses, they are well able to protect the Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas and attain the unimpeded analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*)—of phenomena, meaning, language, and eloquence—expounding the True Dharma without interruption or exhaustion.
In a single kṣaṇa, throughout unspeakably many worlds, he explains all the questions and difficulties raised by sentient beings with a single voice, causing them all to rejoice.

Throughout ten thousand *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, he can manifest the spiritual powers of as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in a million Ganges Rivers; his inexhaustible treasury of Dharma brings benefit to perfection.

"Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva on the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā bhūmi*) employs immeasurable wisdom in contemplation and observation. From the initial arousal of faith, passing through a million *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, he extensively gathers immeasurable factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), increases boundless great merit and wisdom, realizes mastery over karma, and severs the obstacles to supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). In a single thought-moment, he can pervade as many lands as there are atoms in a hundred trillion *asaṃkhyeya* worlds throughout the ten directions. He fully knows the mental activities and the superior, middling, and inferior faculties of all sentient beings, preaching the Three Vehicles for them and causing them all to universally practice the *pāramitās*."
They enter the Buddha’s sphere of activity, his powers, and his fearlessnesses, and accord with the Tathāgata’s transformation of the basis into quiescence. "Good son!
From the initial cultivation of patience up to the diamond-like samādhi, all are termed the subduing of all afflictions."
Through the patient acceptance of non-arising, one illuminates the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), extinguishes all afflictions (*kleśa*), and gives rise to the wisdom of liberation.
By gradually subduing and extinguishing [them], one attains the state of non-arising through the mind of arising and ceasing.
If this mind ceases, then ignorance ceases.
All knowledge and vision prior to the diamond-like concentration (vajropama-samādhi) are not called "vision.
Only the Buddha, through sudden realization and possessing all-knowledge (sarvajñā), possesses all knowledge and vision such that it is rightly termed "vision."

“Good son! When the Vajra-samādhi manifests before one, yet one is still not yet equal to the Unequaled; it is like a person ascending a great high tower, who surveys all things and understands them all without exception.”

In the state of liberation, there is a single characteristic which is the absence of characteristics; it is without arising and without cessation, identical to the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) and equal to the dharma-nature (dharmatā). Having fulfilled the treasury of merit, one abides in the stage of the Tathāgata.

“Good son! These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, who uphold and explain [this teaching], all go to the buddha-fields of the ten directions to benefit and bring peace to sentient beings and to penetrate the true mark;
they are no different from me today.”
“Good son! All Tathāgatas of the ten directions and the entire dharma-realm have attained buddhahood by relying upon this gate;
if one says that buddhahood can be attained by transcending this, it is the teaching of Māra, not the teaching of the Buddha.”
"Therefore, you all should know thus, see thus, and believe and understand thus.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Those Bodhisattvas of the Patience of Subjugation Nurture themselves within the Buddha-dharma."
Firmly establishing the thirty minds is called "non-retrogression.
Having first realized the nature of equality, one is born into the family of all Buddhas;
because of this initial awakening, it is named the Stage of Joy (Pramuditā-bhūmi).
Far removed from defilements and the various stains such as anger,
possessing the purity of ethical discipline and virtue, it is called the Ground of Freedom from Stain (*vimalā-bhūmi*).
Having destroyed the darkness of ignorance and attained all meditative concentrations, it is named the Ground of Freedom from Stain.
Illumination arises from the light of wisdom; it is named the Ground of Radiant Light (*Prabhākārī*).
With the pure factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), one remains far removed from the views of self and what pertains to the self;
as the flame of wisdom blazes intensely, it is named the Ground of Blazing Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī*).
Knowing the truths as they truly are, And all the worldly arts and crafts,
Benefiting sentient beings in manifold ways— This is called the Ground Difficult to Conquer (Sudurjayā).
Observing the phenomena of dependent origination, From ignorance through to old age and death,
Being able to realize that profound depth is called the Ground of Manifestation (Abhimukhī).
Through the samādhi of skillful means, manifesting immeasurable bodies and responding to sentient beings with expertise,
it is called the Ground of Far-Going (Dūraṃgamā).
Abiding in the ocean of signlessness, empowered by all Buddhas,
and possessing the mastery to shatter the armies of Māra— this is called the Immovable Ground (Acalā-bhūmi).
Having attained the four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid), one proclaims everything with a single voice.
All who hear it rejoice; this is called the Ground of Excellent Intelligence (*Sādhumatī-bhūmi*).
Wisdom like dense clouds pervades the entire Dharma-realm;
universally sprinkling the nectar of the Dharma, it is called the Ground of the Dharma-Cloud (*Dharmameghā-bhūmi*).
“Fulfilling the untainted realm (*anāsravadhātu*), with a body of liberation that is eternally pure,
quiescent, and inconceivable— this is called ‘Omniscience’ (*sarvajñatā*).
The Buddha told King Prasenajit:
"After my parinirvāṇa, when the Dharma is about to perish, because all sentient beings commit evil karma, various calamities will arise in all lands.

The kings and others, in order to protect themselves, their crown princes, their sons, their queens and consorts, their retinues, their ministers, their subjects, and their entire kingdoms, should immediately receive and uphold this Prajñāpāramitā; thus they shall all attain peace and happiness."
I entrust this sutra to the kings, and not to the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās. Why is this?
"Without the sovereign power of a king, it cannot be established; therefore, you all must constantly uphold, recite, and explain it. Great King!
The great trichiliocosm that I have now transformed consists of ten billion Sumeru mountains, ten billion suns and moons, and each Sumeru has four continents."

In this Jambudvīpa, consisting of sixteen great nations, five hundred intermediate nations, and one hundred thousand minor nations, should the seven calamities arise within any of these lands, all the kings, for the sake of eliminating those calamities, should uphold and expound this Prajñāpāramitā; then the seven calamities will immediately cease, and the kingdoms will become peaceful and happy.
King Prasenajit asked,
"What are the seven calamities?
The Buddha said:
"First, the sun and moon lose their proper courses.
The color of the sun changes—it becomes white, red, yellow, or black; or two, three, four, or five suns shine simultaneously.
The color of the moon changes—it becomes red or yellow."
The sun and moon may undergo eclipses, or they may appear with double halos—halos of one, two, three, four, or five layers manifesting.
Second, the stars lose their proper courses;
comets, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, Mercury, Saturn, and all other such planets each undergo transformations, or at times appear during the day.
Third, the fires of dragons, ghosts, humans, and trees break out on all four sides, burning and consuming all things.
Fourth, the seasons change irregularly, and cold and heat become unstable.

Thunder and lightning occurred in winter; frost, ice, and snow fell in summer; mountains of earth and stone, as well as sand and gravel, rained down; unseasonable hail fell; red and black water poured forth; rivers overflowed their banks, carrying stones and floating mountains.
Fifth, violent winds arise frequently, obscuring the sun and moon, tearing down houses and uprooting trees, and blowing sand and rolling stones.
Sixth, heaven and earth suffer from extreme drought; ponds and pools dry up, plants and trees wither and die, and the hundred grains fail to ripen.
Seventh, enemies from the four quarters will invade the country and its borders, and as weapons clash in competition, the common people will perish.
"Great King!
I have now briefly described these various calamities."
There were days when the sun did not appear, and nights when the moon did not appear;
there were various celestial calamities, such as the absence of clouds, rain, or snow;
and there were various terrestrial calamities, such as the earth splitting open and quaking, or even blood flowing.
Spirits and deities will appear, and birds and beasts will act strangely.
When such calamities arise in measureless and boundless numbers, for each and every disaster that occurs, one must uphold, recite, and explain this Prajñāpāramitā.
At that time, when the sixteen kings heard what the Buddha had said, they were all struck with alarm and fear.
King Prasenajit addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"For what reason do such calamities exist in heaven and earth?
The Buddha said,
"Great King!"
Because all the people in the great and small kingdoms and towns of Jambudvīpa are unfilial toward their parents and disrespectful toward their teachers, elders, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas;
and because kings and ministers do not practice the True Dharma, these calamities arise due to such evils.

“Great King! The *prajñāpāramitā* can give birth to all the dharmas of the Buddhas, all the dharmas of liberation for Bodhisattvas, all the unsurpassed dharmas of kings, and all the dharmas of transcendence for sentient beings. It is like a *maṇi* jewel whose substance possesses manifold virtues: it can subdue venomous dragons and various malevolent spirits; it can fulfill the heart’s desires of people; it is called the ‘Wish-Fulfilling Jewel’ (*cintāmaṇi*) by the Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*); it can cause the great dragon kings such as Nanda and Upananda to send down sweet rain to moisten and nourish the grasses and trees; and if placed atop a high banner during the dark night, its light illuminates heaven and earth, as bright as the rising sun.”

This Prajñāpāramitā is likewise so; you kings should fashion jeweled victory banners, pennants, and canopies, making extensive offerings by burning incense and scattering flowers. Place the scripture within a jeweled casket and set it upon a jeweled table. When you wish to travel, always lead it before you; at whatever place you dwell, construct a canopy of the seven jewels and provide a seat of various gems, placing the scripture upon it and honoring it with all manner of offerings as if serving one's parents, or as the devas serve Śakra, Lord of the Gods.
"Great King!
I see that all the human kings of various nations have become emperors because they served, honored, and made offerings to five hundred Buddhas in past lives;
furthermore, all the sages who have attained the fruits of the Path come to be born in their kingdoms to bring about great benefit."
"When a king’s merit is exhausted and he lacks the Way, the sages will depart and calamities will arise in competition.

Great King! If, in future ages, there are kings who establish the True Dharma and protect the Triple Gem, I shall cause the assembly of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas from the five directions to go and protect their kingdoms."
"In the east, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi, holding a vajra and emitting blue light, shall go with four koṭis of bodhisattvas to protect that land."
"In the south, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajraratna holds a vajra-maṇi and emits light with the color of the sun; together with four koṭis of bodhisattvas, he shall go to protect that land."
"In the west, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajratīkṣṇa, holding a vajra-sword and emitting golden light, shall go with four koṭis of bodhisattvas to protect that land."
"In the north, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrayakṣa, holding a vajra-bell and emitting light the color of lapis lazuli, shall go with four koṭis of yakṣas to protect that land."
"The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Central-Diamond-Pāramitā, holding a vajra-wheel and emitting five-colored light, shall go with four koṭis of bodhisattvas to protect that land."
"These five bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, each accompanied by such an immeasurable great assembly, shall bring great benefit to your kingdom;
you should fashion their images and make offerings to them."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi and the others rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and, withdrawing to one side, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

By our original vows and sustained by the Buddha’s spiritual power, wherever in all the lands of the worlds of the ten directions this sutra is upheld, recited, or explained, we shall each, together with such retinues, arrive at that place in a single thought-moment. We shall protect the True Dharma and establish the True Dharma, ensuring that no calamities or disasters occur within those realms, and that all violence, warfare, pestilence, and epidemics are entirely eliminated.
“World-Honored One!
I possess a dhāraṇī capable of providing empowerment and protection; it is the swift gateway through which all Buddhas have practiced in the past.

If anyone hears it but once with their ears, all their karmic obstructions and hindrances will be completely extinguished, let alone those who recite and study it until they master it. By the majestic power of this Dharma, it shall cause the realm to be forever free from all calamities.”
Then, before the Buddha, they spoke this dhāraṇī with one voice:
"Namo ratnatrayāya. Namo ’ryāvalokiteśvarāya."

*Pra-mi-ti svāhā.* (36) At that time, having heard these words, the World-Honored One praised Vajrapāṇi and the other bodhisattvas, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"

If there be anyone who recites and upholds this dhāraṇī, I and all the Buddhas of the ten directions shall constantly provide protection; all malevolent spirits and ghosts will revere them as they would a Buddha, and before long, they shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“Great King!
I entrust this sutra to you all:

the kings of the kingdoms of Vaiśālī, Kośala, Śrāvastī, Magadha, Vārāṇasī, Kapilavastu, Kuśinagara, Kauśāmbī, Pañcāla, Pāṭaliputra, Mathurā, Oḍḍiyāna, Puṇḍravardhana, Devavardhana, Kāśī, and Campā—all such kings as these should receive, uphold, and practice the Prajñāpāramitā.”
At that time, the great assembly, including the asuras, heard the Buddha describe these various calamities; their hair stood on end, and they cried out in a loud voice:
"May we not be born in that land in the future!"

At that time, the sixteen kings immediately renounced their royal thrones to cultivate the path of renunciation; they perfected the eight bases of mastery and the ten spheres of totality, and attained the patience of subduing, the patience of faith, and the patience of the non-arising of dharmas.

At that time, the entire assembly of devas and humans, asuras, and others, scattered mandārava flowers, mañjūṣaka flowers, vārṣika flowers, and sumanā flowers as offerings to the Buddha; according to their respective dispositions, they attained the three gates of liberation, the emptiness of beings, the emptiness of phenomena, and the factors of enlightenment.

Immeasurable and innumerable bodhisattva-mahāsattvas scattered *kuṇḍuka* flowers and *padma* flowers as an offering to the Buddha; immeasurable samādhis all became manifest before them, and they attained the stage of compliance with patience (*ānulomikī-kṣānti*) and the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Immeasurable and innumerable bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attained as many gates of samādhi as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River; they realized the equality of the ultimate and conventional truths, possessed unimpeded analytical knowledge, and constantly gave rise to great compassion. Throughout worlds as numerous as the atoms within hundreds of thousands of millions of asaṃkhyeya buddha-fields, they extensively benefited sentient beings and manifested their bodies as Buddhas.
The Buddha told King Prasenajit:
"I now exhort you all!

After my parinirvāṇa, when the True Dharma is about to perish—in the final fifty years, the final five hundred years, and the final five thousand years—there will be no Buddha, no Dharma, and no Saṃgha."

I entrust this sutra and the Three Jewels to the various kings to establish and protect them, so that my fourfold assembly of disciples may receive, uphold, read, and recite it, understand its principles, and extensively proclaim the essential teachings for the sake of sentient beings, leading them to practice and transcend birth and death.
“Great King!

In the future age of the five turbidities, all kings, princes, and ministers, relying on their own high status, will destroy my teaching and openly establish restrictive laws to constrain my disciples.”
It is not permitted for bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs to leave the household life to practice the Right Path, nor is it permitted for them to construct stūpas or images of the Buddha.
For laypeople to occupy high seats while bhikṣus stand upon the ground is no different from the laws governing soldiers and slaves.
"You should know that at that time, the Dharma will not long remain.
Great King! The causes and conditions for the destruction of your kingdom were all created by you yourself."
Relying on their own power and authority, they suppressed the fourfold assembly and forbade them from cultivating merit.
Various wicked bhikṣus accepted special invitations for private feasts.
Wise bhikṣus, however, remained of one mind, maintaining mutual affection and kindness, and sought merit through communal assemblies for the upoṣadha.
These are the teachings of external paths; they are not at all my instruction.
When the common people suffer from epidemics and immeasurable hardships and calamities, you should know that at such a time the kingdom will be destroyed.
"Great King!

In the final age of the Dharma, kings, ministers, and the fourfold assembly of disciples will each act contrary to the Dharma, falsely attributing various faults to the Buddha’s teachings. They will bind bhikṣus with what is neither Dharma nor Vinaya, treating them like prisoners in a jail."
"You should know that at that time, the Dharma will not remain for long.
Great King!

After my parinirvāṇa, the fourfold assembly of disciples, as well as all kings, princes, and officials who are the ones entrusted with upholding and protecting the Triple Gem, will themselves bring about their own destruction. They are like parasites within a lion's body that eat the lion's own flesh; they are not outsiders."

Those who destroy my Dharma shall incur great transgression: the True Dharma will decline and become thin; the people will lack correct conduct; all evils will gradually increase; their lifespans will diminish day by day; there will no longer be filial sons; the six relations will be disharmonious; devas and nāgas will not grant their protection; evil spirits and malevolent dragons will daily come to inflict harm; calamities and anomalies will succeed one another as disasters run rampant; they shall fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts; and even if they should obtain human form, they will be poor, lowly, and deficient in their faculties—just as a shadow follows a form, as an echo responds to a sound, or as characters remain visible after a lamp is extinguished while one writes at night, so too are the retributions for destroying the Dharma.
"Great King!

In future ages, all kings, princes, and ministers shall arbitrarily establish registers for my disciples, appointing officials and masters to oversee the senior and junior *saṃghasthaviras*, and employ them against the principles of justice."
"You should know that at such a time, the Buddha-dharma will not remain for long.
Great King!
In future ages, all kings and the fourfold assembly of disciples shall establish and propagate [the teachings] by relying upon the path constantly practiced by all Buddhas of the ten directions."
Yet evil bhikṣus, seeking fame and profit, do not rely upon my Dharma; they speak of their own faults before kings, creating conditions for the destruction of the Dharma.
Those kings, failing to discern the truth, believe and accept these words, arbitrarily establishing restrictive laws that do not conform to the Buddha’s precepts.
"You should know that at such a time, the Dharma will not remain for long.

Great King! In future ages, kings, ministers, and the fourfold assembly of disciples will themselves create the causes and conditions for the destruction of the Dharma and the ruin of the nation; they shall suffer the consequences in their own persons, and it shall not be the fault of the Buddha-Dharma."
"The devas and nāgas have departed, and the five corruptions are increasingly rampant; were one to explain this in full detail, it would not be exhausted even at the end of an eon.

At that time, when the sixteen great kings heard these various admonitions for the future, they wept and wailed in grief, their voices shaking the trichiliocosm until heaven and earth grew dark and the radiance of light vanished.

At that time, the various kings each received and upheld the Buddha’s words with a sincere heart, resolving not to prohibit the fourfold assembly from leaving home to study the Way, but rather to act in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching.
Then, a great multitude as numerous as the sands of the Ganges all sighed together, saying:
"At such a time, the world will be empty and void; it will be an age without a Buddha."
At that time, King Prasenajit addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
What should this sutra be named?"
"How should we receive and uphold it?
The Buddha told the Great King:

"This sutra is named 'The Prajñāpāramitā for Benevolent Kings Protecting the State,' and it may also be called 'The Ambrosial Medicine of the Dharma. If there are those who consume and practice it, it can heal all ailments."
“Great King!

The merits of the Prajñāpāramitā are like space, immeasurable and unfathomable. If there are those who uphold, receive, read, and recite it, the merits they obtain will protect you, O Benevolent King, as well as all sentient beings, like a surrounding wall and like city ramparts; therefore, you all should uphold it.”

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the immeasurable bodhisattva-mahāsattvas such as Maitreya and Siṃhanāda, the immeasurable śrāvakas such as Śāriputra and Subhūti, the immeasurable devas and humans of the desire realm and the form realm, the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, asuras, and the entire great assembly, having heard what the Buddha had preached, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
